title: The Weavers' Count of Brides
author: Orrin Vasse, for the Bride-Weavers of Isseva
body:
# Brides walked out

*Cut on a withy tally and copied onto a board for the Council, who asked.*

---

The fortieth of my binding. Walked out at the spring tide, faced to the water, arms out. Knots in the hem: more than I counted.

The thirty-ninth, gone grey and fallen at the midsummer, as they do.

The third week after the walking-out: found turned. Faced to the land. Feet in the same holes. Hem wet to the knee.

*Under it, in another hand:* The drowned stood before her that night, eleven of them. Ollan says twelve. I say eleven, and one more that was only standing behind them, a big man in a sailor's coat, with his back to us, looking at the sea.

title: Forty Jars
author: Ferrit Oache
body:
# The jars, by number

*Chalked on the inside of the catcher's door.*

---

1 to 12: the North Fen, the dark of the moon after the thaw. Small. Steady.

13 to 30: the Gullhithe flats. Brighter. They hum when the tide is in.

31 to 39: off the Moreva boards, where the lanterns go out over the water. These turn to face Moreva and will not be turned.

40: big. Off the Gullhithe flats at the autumn spring tide. Cracked its jar the first night and went.

*Under it, smaller:* The wild ones visit the 31s most. Do not think about why.

title: The Tide-Watchers' Book
author: the Tide-Watchers of Oulea
body:
# Spring tides at the needle

*A tarred book kept in a box at the gauge's foot; the first leaves are in a hand nobody can read any more.*

---

*Hesk Vaurel's hand:* Spring tide, the thaw. Float at the hundred-and-sixty-third notch. Two fingers over my mother's last.

Spring tide, midsummer. The hundred-and-sixty-third again.

Spring tide, the autumn. The hundred-and-sixty-fourth. Saltgate's gates went the same night; I heard them from here.

*Lower down:* Somebody has cut a notch above mine. Not me. Not any watcher. No mark.

*Lowest of all, pressed hard:* The line is the flood. I am as sure of it as of my boots. Hush, Hesk.

title: The Hask Book of Names
author: the Hasks, ropewalkers
body:
# Names walked

*A long narrow book, every line a rope: the buyer, the name walked into it, the walker.*

---

Mooring, forty paces, for the Isseva burial jetty: walked with OLLAN VAUSE, by Corra.

Lantern-line, the Causeway, for Lissane: walked with all the names she gave, which took the morning, by Corra.

Boat-rope, for a Moreva eel-man: walked with his drowned wife's name, by Corra. He cried at the wheel. They do.

*In an older hand, nine years back:* For Iven Hask, when he comes home. Walked by Iven Hask, with his own name, for luck, the morning he went to the Outfall.

*Under it, newer, in Corra's:* Still on the rack.

title: A Scrap on the Pole
author: unsigned
body:
*A scrap of indigo cloth tied among the ribbons on the Unwinding's pole, written on in charcoal:*

I walked it five times round and said it and it did not go.

I walked it again.

I will walk it until it goes, or until I do.

title: Flights for the Council
author: Pell Oduin, heron-reader
body:
# Readings of the North Fen herons

*Copied off the slate every evening into a book the Council never sends for.*

---

The thaw: east, to Oulnauve. Something new at the stakes. (The Callers.)

The new moon: north and east, to the tower on the North Shore, round it six times. (The Sounding.)

The spring tide: west to the Builders' needle at Oulea, and stood along its plinth facing the sea, every one.

This week: west, to the old water past the Saltgate, the Salt Isles' barrow. Half came back.

*Under it:* Herons do not drown.

title: The Mother's Feeding
author: Nelle Saye
body:
# What she has been fed

*A tally on a board by the tub, in the herb-wife's hand.*

---

An eel, every Fifthday, sixty years; my grandmother's strokes, my mother's, mine.

This spring: an eel, and she closed on it before it dropped.

An eel, and she closed on the tweezers.

Nothing, the week after; I didn't. She grew a hand that week anyway.

*Under it, crossed through and written again:* The boot was on the rim in the morning. I have not fed her since. She has not needed it.

title: The Dredge's Last Shift
author: Brannoc Tull, dredge-master, for the Tallymen's Guild
body:
# Shift-book of the Great Dredge

*Guild ruling, Guild ink, a dredge-master's careful hand that gets less careful.*

---

Day 41. Broke through to the Builders' street at eight metres. Dry. Black stone, dead straight. Engineers below. The Guild will want this.

Day 44. A hall at the street's end, roof on. Doors off the street both sides, all shut. Water behind the doors; you can hear it.

Day 46. Opened the third door on the left to see. Water came through to the knee and went down again. Nothing else. Kettle the younger says something went past his legs.

Day 47. Change of shift. Taking the day men down to bring the night men up together. Faster. Corley will complain. Let her.

*The last line, not in his hand:* the chain will do for climbing

title: The Keel-King's Grave-Roll
author: the Salt Isles, in their own tongue, glossed in Sedgish
body:
# Who sails with the king

*Scratched on a board of grey driftwood among the grave-goods, the Salt Isles' runes with a reedfolk gloss under every line.*

---

Hrothe Tidecaller, king of the four isles, who died in the reed country of the eel-fever. His ship *Gull-Breast* with him, dragged up the flats on rollers by two hundred men, sunk in the last dry ground.

His crew with him at their oars, forty, who swore it.

*The gloss:* So the sea must come up the land to fetch him home. That was the bargain with the sea: you shall have him back, but you must come for him.

*At the foot, newer, scratched with a knife:* IVEN HASK, of Isseva, who came down to ship and was asked aboard. Forty-one.
